1:
Keil and Delitzsch date the oracle two months less six days after the preceding one and lay out its plan: the question whom Pharaoh resembles, Assyria depicted as a towering cedar, that cedar felled by the prince of the nations for its height and pride, and the mourning of everything at its fall; the question returns at the end, with the conclusion that Pharaoh will perish likewise. The reminiscence of that empire and its destruction, they add, was well adapted to overthrow all reliance on the might of Egypt. Henry finds the comfort in the timing: the people of God were then in the depth of their distress, and it would relieve them, and check the insolence of their neighbours, to know that the cup was going round and would shortly pass into the hands of those who hated them.

Henry makes the question a piece of moral psychology. We are apt to judge of ourselves by comparison, and those who think highly of themselves fancy themselves equal to the celebrated. God allows the comparison, he says, but adds that whoever is chosen will be found to have had a day of falling, the ruin of others being set before us lest we think we stand out of danger. Ellicott notes that the word for the multitude means literally tumult and takes in whatever occasions it, their wealth, their idols and every source of pride; Wesley reads simply numerous subjects.

Who the cedar is has divided the readers. Clarke asks why the Assyrian should be introduced in a chapter about Egypt, and follows an authority who renders the phrase the tall or very stately cedar, so that the whole description belongs to Egypt from the start. Gill keeps the Assyrian and hesitates only over which, the monarchy itself or one of its last kings, the empire having lasted from the days of Nimrod down to a few years before; he reports two ancient versions that give cypress for cedar, and rejects them, since the cypress did not grow in Lebanon. Ellicott adds that Lebanon is named only because the most famous cedars grew there, Assyria having once possessed it but never made it a seat of empire; and he takes the thick boughs of the English for the clouds. Henry notes that in the old fable the fruit-bearing trees refused promotion, so the choice fell on the cedar, which is stately and casts a great shadow but bears no fruit.

The waters that made him great are read locally. Gill takes them for the Tigris beside Nineveh and the traffic it carried; Clarke for the overflowing of the Nile, and then, since waters often mean peoples, for the nations under Egyptian rule; Wesley for the sea sending out the rivers that watered him, the plants about the tree being the provinces. Ellicott corrects plants to plantation and takes the little rivers for the subordinate nations nourished from the stream of prosperity that swelled the empire.

Henry works the description into three heads: the cedar was tall, spreading and serviceable. It overtopped every tree of the field, and its branches ran out as far as they ran up, its large dominions kept in shape like a tree well ordered by a gardener; and it sheltered every creature that came to it, which he turns into a rule that those who have power ought to use it for the protection of those they have power over, though the utmost security any creature can give is only the shadow of a tree. On the garden of God, Ellicott is careful that Assyria is not placed in it but only compared with its trees, though the comparison may have been suggested by the traditional site of Eden falling within the Assyrian bounds. Henry closes on the envy of the trees of Eden, that those who excel make themselves the objects of envy.
10:
Gill marks the turn: the greatness described, now the fall and its cause, pride. Ellicott observes that although the fall was already past it is partly spoken of in the future, which makes the whole more graphic and may also be because the object of the parable is not Assyria but Egypt, whose fall was still to come; Assyria is addressed directly at the outset and in the third person afterwards. Henry makes that pride the link between the two kings, since as face answers to face in a glass so does one carnal heart to another; the oppression of the people of God is charged on Egyptian and Assyrian alike, but here traced to its cause, for when men outward condition rises their minds rise with it, a humble spirit being rare in the midst of great advancement.

Who the mighty one of the heathen was, nobody agrees. Gill canvasses three, Arbaces the Mede who defeated Sardanapalus, Merodachbaladan of Babylon who vanquished Esarhaddon, and, as he prefers, Nebuchadnezzar, who with the king of Media took Nineveh in the first year of his reign. Clarke names Nebuchadnezzar and notes that this fell some twenty years before the prophecy, which is why the Assyrian of the earlier verse may after all be meant. Ellicott names the father instead, since at the time of the fall of Assyria the Chaldean monarch was Nabopolassar; and Wesley names Arbaces, who could bring four hundred thousand Medes, Persians, Babylonians and Arabians together.

Henry follows the figure down. The stately cedar was first cropped, the terrible of the nations being soldiers armed and commissioned to destroy, who lopped its branches by taking province after province, so that in highland and lowland and along the rivers countries were broken off from the empire; its feathers were borrowed, and when every bird had fetched back its own it stood naked as a stump. Then it was deserted, those who had fled to it going down from its shadow when it could no longer protect them, which he turns into a warning that great men should not be proud of a retinue that attends them only for what it can get. Gill makes the strangers the Medes, living at a distance, and the terrible of the nations the soldiers of the Babylonian army.

Then the fall is insulted over. Ellicott sees no inconsistency between the nations rushing away and gathering on the trunk afterwards: they flee the catastrophe, then come back to fatten on the ruin. Gill reads the returning birds as the peoples who had sought the empire protection now preying on its provinces, and adds that one authority took the verse literally, of birds and beasts feeding on the carcasses of the slain, which he thinks no bad reading. Henry gives the reverse side, that the fallen trees of Eden are comforted in the nether world to see this proud cedar brought as low as themselves, while the trees of Lebanon still standing mourn, reading their own destiny in his fall.

The stated purpose closes the passage. Gill takes it as a warning to kings ruling multitudes comparable to waters, not to be elated by their grandeur nor insolent toward God nor oppressive toward their subjects. Clarke draws the lesson wider, that however elevated a state may be God can bring it down, pride having his peculiar abhorrence; it does not suit the sons of men, since it made devils of angels and makes fiends of men. Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering, that the trees shall no longer stand upon themselves for their height, relying on their own strength and infatuated by the prosperity given them, and notes that the constant mention of water may carry a covert allusion to Egypt made fertile by the Nile. Wesley reads the trees as emperors and kings, and the children of men as common persons of no distinction.
15:
Ellicott maps the mourning back on to the description. The deep that is covered is the same flood of waters that fertilised the great cedar, the floods are the rivers of the earlier verse and the great waters its multitude of waters, so that the sources of the empire prosperity are stopped as the whole is put into mourning; the word rendered mourn means literally to be black, which suits the figure of Lebanon better than the English does, and the trees of the field that faint are the subordinate potentates dismayed at the fall. Gill takes the going down to the grave for the destruction of the monarchy, the king stripped of majesty and authority and as one dead. Clarke reads the mourning of Lebanon as the lament of all the confederates, and Wesley guesses at portentous signs in the sea and the rivers and among the trees.

Gill supplies the noise. As a large cedar felled in Lebanon was heard at a distance, so the fall of this monarchy was heard far and near, and the kings of the nations shook for fear that they should fall in the same way. Ellicott notes that the hell of the English is here, as generally, the world of the departed, and thinks a passage of another prophet on the same theme was in the writer mind. Wesley catches the strangeness of the comfort: the words are spoken to the dead in the manner of the living, who rejoice to see the proud brought low, and the trees comforted are all kings and particularly the greatest, all that drink water being those who enjoyed great power and riches.

Those who went down with him are read as his own people. Gill names his nobles, princes, generals and soldiers; Wesley his neighbouring kings, and his arm as the loyal subjects on whom he relied and by whom he acted; Clarke says only that they went into remediless destruction.

The closing question applies the whole. Gill has it put to Pharaoh directly: name whichever potentate you please, name the Assyrian just described, though you are not his equal; and if you were, it would not secure you, since he fell and so will you. Ellicott says the chapter is brought to a point here, Egypt being like Assyria in glory and therefore to be like her in the experience of the judgments of God. Wesley adds that the lying down is as one unclean, despised and under a curse. Clarke agrees that the whole allegory of the lofty cedar refers to Pharaoh and his people, but records an authority who understood the entire chapter of the king of Assyria, with Egypt only shadowed under it, and who quoted the old tag that the name need only be changed and the tale is told of you.
